newsitem.title: UK: Foreign exchange market, recalling past crises, stalks Czech crown.
newsitem.headline: Foreign exchange market, recalling past crises, stalks Czech crown.

text.p: The Czech central bank's move to replenish foreign exchange reserves after an unsuccessful bid to defend the crown in May will do little to throw traders off the scent of crown instability, analysts said.
The Czech National Bank said on Thursday it had arranged a $1.5 billion one-year revolving credit facility with four international banks in order to bolster its reserves.

Yet strategists said the parallels with currency crises in western Europe during the summers of 1992 and 1993 grow clearer every day and in an environment like this, big central bank warchests increasingly buy blanks, they said.
"The level of foreign exchange reserves is simply not going to change the basic story here," said Avinash Persaud, head of currency research at JP Morgan.

The market still perceives contradictions in Czech economic policy and views the government there as increasingly fragile. Most of all, it sees the penal interest rates imposed to shore up the crown last month as ultimately unsustainable.

"The government is proposing to cut public spending by 3 percent of GDP at a time when the economy is slowing rapidly and interest rates are at unrealistic levels," said Persaud. "This can't persist. Neither domestic companies nor investors can plan ahead in an environment of inherent instability."
The government of Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus barely survived a confidence vote in parliament Tuesday to push through an emergency package of economic austerity measure.

The crown, meantime, has lost almost 10 percent of its value against a trade weighted basket of currencies since the central bank was forced to allow the currency to float freely on May 27 after a wave of adverse speculation.

Analysts estimate that prior to the float the central bnak haemorhagged between $1 bilion and $3 billion of reserves in a futile attempt to maintain crown's 7.5 percent fluctuation bands either side of a foxed peg to the dollar and German mark.
CNB reserves were just over $11 billion at the end of April.

"The Czech credit facility smacks of the UK move in 1992, when it borrowed 16 billion Ecu as a signal of its intent to defend sterling in the ERM," said one emerging markets trader at a UK bank in London. "We all know what happened then."
The UK and Italy were forced to abandon membership of the European exchange rate mechanism in September of 1992 and allow sterling and the lira to depreciate sharply.

The crown has stabilised since the May 27 collapse and firmed from its lows but this is because interest rates have remained at extreme levels. The central bnak has only allowed rates to edge back lower.

The bank's two-week reverse repurchase rate slipped to 29 percent Wednesday from 39 percent on Monday. But the emergency Lombard rate remains at 50 percent, up from 14 percent before the May crisis, and informal central bank restrictions of overseas access to crown liquidity remain.

"The problem with these sorts of interest rate levels is that they're damned if the do (cut them) and damned if they don't," said Jonathan Hoffmann, director - economics at CS First Boston in London. "People are just waiting for these rates to come down before going short crowns again."
The wave of speculation against ERM currencies in 1992 hinged on the unsustainability of the interest-rate levels needed to protect existing ERM currency pegs.
High interest rates are a deterrent to overseas speculators who look to borrow currency to sell short for profit, but as soon as these rates come down again the temptation returns.

In the meantime, highly leveraged domestic Czech companies will feel the squeeze of such high borrowing costs and this will exaggerate the economic downturn, putting more pressure onthe crown and on the government to act or step down.

One option is to reintroduce formal exchange controls similar to the Thai authorities, who have effectively created a two-tier market of onshore and offshore bahts to prevent a similar attack on the baht last month recurring.
Analysts are sceptical the Czechs will go down that route, however.

"The Czech Republic has strong European Union ambitions and with that comes a more liberal way of thinking about capital controls," said Persaud at JP Morgan. "To take that option now would only store up problems for a later date and end up damaging investor confidence in the longer-term."
